sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four. Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: A chosen cuddly toy in place of the dummy, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest; avoid stopping suddenly. An Australian state health page, used as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (NHS)
sources.quote: Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. Praise times without the dummy. Keep it out of sight and reach. Parents and carers, including childcare settings, should follow the same steps so the message is consistent. Try to remove the dummy once they are asleep.
sources.supports: New ways to soothe, a dummy fairy, praise, keep it out of sight, the same steps from every carer. An NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being 'dummy free'. Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child's sight. Using distraction techniques can help when asked for bottles or dummies.
sources.supports: Set a dummy free date, keep dummies out of sight, distraction when the child asks. An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four. Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: A chosen cuddly toy in place of the dummy, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest; avoid stopping suddenly. An Australian state health page, used as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (NHS)
sources.quote: Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. Praise times without the dummy. Keep it out of sight and reach. Parents and carers, including childcare settings, should follow the same steps so the message is consistent. Try to remove the dummy once they are asleep.
sources.supports: New ways to soothe, a dummy fairy, praise, keep it out of sight, the same steps from every carer. An NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being 'dummy free'. sources.supports: Set a dummy free date, keep dummies out of sight, distraction when the child asks. An NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (reviewed 12 Jun 2026)
sources.quote: Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four. Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (NHS)
sources.quote: Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. Parents and carers, including childcare settings, should follow the same steps so the message is consistent. Try to remove the dummy once they are asleep.
sources.supports: New ways to soothe, a dummy fairy, praise, keep it out of sight, the same steps from every carer. An NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Toilet Training (Potty Training)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Instead of using age, look for signs that your child may be ready to start heading for the potty. Don't make your child sit on the toilet against their will. Establish a routine. Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed.
sources.supports: Look for readiness signs, never sit a child on the toilet against their will, a routine (for example after waking or after drinking, a few minutes), praise every attempt, no punishment for accidents.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 6 Nov 2023)
sources.quote: Pick a potty-chair. Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. Be a role model. Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. Choose positive words your family will use to describe body parts, urine and bowel movements. Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. When toilet training starts, switch to big-kid underwear. Avoid a power struggle. Remember that children control when and where they pee and poop. Understand their fear. To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet.
sources.supports: Potty chair that fits, role model, words, morning routine, big-kid underwear, no power struggle, understand fear and let the child flush.

sources.title: Create a Potty Training Plan for Your Child

אתם אומרים שהיום אין טיטול,
ואני מרגיש גדול וקצת מבולבל.

לשבת על הסיר כבר עכשיו, בבוקר.

הסיר שלי, בגובה שלי
הרגליים שלי על הרצפה,
ואני יושב יציב.
אני מספר לדובי סיפור,
ולפעמים לא קורה כלום.
וזה גם בסדר.

מה קורה מאחורי הדלת?
אתם נכנסים לשירותים וסוגרים.
ואני עומד בחוץ, סקרן.
אם תתנו לי לראות פעם אחת,
אני אבין מה עושים שם,
ואיך שוטפים ידיים אחרי.

עוד מעט צריך לנסות
שתיתי כוס מיץ גדולה בגינה.
אתם מסתכלים על השעון,
ואומרים לי ״ננסה רגע?״
״גיא, הסיר מחכה לך. כמה דקות.״

פספוס על השטיח

שלולית, ומכנסיים רטובים.

״בפעם הבאה נצליח״, וננגב ביחד.

״איזה יום, גיא! ניסית כל כך יפה.״

sources.title: Toilet Training (Potty Training)
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Instead of using age, look for signs that your child may be ready to start heading for the potty. Don't make your child sit on the toilet against their will. Establish a routine. Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed.
sources.supports: Look for readiness signs, never sit a child on the toilet against their will, a routine (for example after waking or after drinking, a few minutes), praise every attempt, no punishment for accidents.

sources.title: Potty Training: 12 Tips to Keep the Process Positive
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 6 Nov 2023)
sources.quote: Pick a potty-chair. Children's feet should be able to reach the floor. Be a role model. Let your children see you use the toilet and wash your hands afterward. Choose positive words your family will use to describe body parts, urine and bowel movements. Make a habit of seating your children onto the potty-chair first thing in the morning. When toilet training starts, switch to big-kid underwear. Avoid a power struggle. Remember that children control when and where they pee and poop. Understand their fear. To give your children a feeling of control, let them flush the toilet.
sources.supports: Potty chair that fits, role model, words, morning routine, big-kid underwear, no power struggle, understand fear and let the child flush.

sources.title: Create a Potty Training Plan for Your Child
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022)
sources.quote: Keep their bathroom routine as consistent as possible, with their potty in the same place every day. When they progress, give them a hug, some praise, and perhaps even a small tangible reward. Tell them you're sure they'll do better next time and ask them to help you clean up.
sources.supports: A consistent routine, praise for progress, and a calm response to an accident (ask the child to help clean up).
